place: Jericho oasis (town or district, no finer place)

feature: Southern part of Jebel Quruntul facing the Jericho plain, down to Wadi el-Qelt: 21 of 22 shelters and caves showed no signs of human activity; the table lists burial caves, one with ossuary fragments outside it and one rock-cut with remains of loculi; a coin of Alexander Jannaeus was found in a wadi bed without context.
period: coin 103–76 BCE; burial caves not dated by the report

place: Tell el-Qos
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: SWP's whole entry reads 'Tell el Kos … Resembles the last'; the previous entry, Tell el Jurn, is 'heaps of stones', not a true tell.
quote: Heaps of stones. It is not a 'Tell' in the strict meaning of the word.

place: Tell el-Qos
source: Milik, J.T., DJD III (1962), section D 'Sites et monuments'
feature: Milik places Bet ha-Qos at the hill called Tell el-Qos where Wadi el-Qelt leaves modern Jericho (citing SWP and Augustinović pp.89–92, not seen here); he describes no remains.
quote: C'est donc là, malgré l'incertitude phonétique, qu'on placera Bet ha-Qos de 3Q15.

place: Tell el-Qos
source: Milik, J.T., DJD III (1962), section D 'Sites et monuments'
feature: Along Wadi el-Qelt beyond modern Jericho, traces of an important canal that looks Byzantine but may have existed in the Roman period.
quote: qui semble byzantin, mais qui existait peut-être déjà à l'époque romaine

place: Tell el-Qos
source: Høgenhaven, J., The Cave 3 Copper Scroll: A Symbolic Journey (2020)
feature: Høgenhaven reports Milik's location 'tentatively'.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in G.J. Brooke and P.R. Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies (2002/2004)
feature: The fortress on Ras Qarantal is identified with Hasmonaean Doq/Dagon; an aqueduct from a small waterfall fed a group of nine rock-cut cisterns belonging to the fortress.
quote: This fortress is identified with Doq or Dagon of the Hasmonaean Period.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in G.J. Brooke and P.R. Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies (2002/2004)
feature: General statement on the desert fortresses near Qumran: all had aqueducts and cisterns and were garrisoned in the 1st century CE.
quote: During the first century CE these fortresses were guarded by Roman soldiers.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: On the summit (Tahunet el-Hawa): foundations of a fortress and a small chapel, and a rock-cut fosse; SWP saw no cisterns and judged the visible buildings medieval.
period: medieval visible remains; earlier occupation possible
quote: There is little doubt that the buildings are mediaeval, though the site may have been occupied earlier.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Milik, J.T., DJD III (1962), section D 'Sites et monuments'
feature: The summit carried the Hasmonean fortress Dok of 1 Macc 16:15, replaced by the monastery of Douka in the 4th century; later building has erased it except for a few architectural pieces (citing Augustinović).
quote: ont oblitéré les traces de la forteresse, à quelques pièces d'architecture près

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: SWP put Docus near ʿAin Duk at Kh. Abu Lahm: remains of a wall and ditch, traces of a small tower, many grain pits (metamir) round a Muslim shrine, and house ruins that 'appear to be modern'; a Roman road descends to ʿAin Duk.
period: wall and tower undated; road Roman
quote: remains of a rude wall and ditch

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Aronshtam, A., 'Region V: Survey and Excavations of Caves along the Jebel Qurunṭul Escarpment between Wadi Abu Saraj and Wadi Ḥalq er-Rummana', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Caves of the Jebel Quruntul escarpment: Late Hellenistic pottery, and a cave used in the 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE with Hasmonean and Herodian coins.
period: Late Hellenistic; 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Eisenberg, E., 'The Excavation of Cave V/49', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: A cave in the northern cliff of Jebel Quruntul used for dwelling and food storage from the 1st c. BCE to the First Revolt; a neighbouring dwelling cave was hewn in the Second Temple period.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Abeles, T., 'Region VII: Survey and Excavations of Caves along the Eastern Escarpment of Jebel Qurunṭul', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Caves in the eastern cliffs of Jebel Quruntul facing Jericho: in one, Roman pottery, fragments of scale armour, a coin of Tiberius struck under the prefect Valerius Gratus and a Nabataean coin; monks' cells of the Qarantal monastery.
period: Roman (coin 17–24 CE); Byzantine to modern monastic use

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Yitah, M., Kam, Y. and Ben-Haim, R., 'Region X: Survey and Excavations of Caves in the Fault Escarpment South of Almog Junction and West of Qalya', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Comparison: the Jebel Quruntul caves were used intensively over long periods, tracking the history of Jericho.
quote: the caves of Jebel Quruntul are a mirror image of the history of the city of Jericho (transl.)

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)
source: Wexler, L., 'Preface', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Dok listed among the desert forts above Jericho (citing Amit 1989, 'The water system of the Dok fortress').

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in G.J. Brooke and P.R. Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies (2002/2004)
feature: Aqueducts of Wadi el-Qelt: the earliest in the Judaean desert, north of the wadi, fed the Hasmonaean palace and Royal Estate; Herod built a Qelt aqueduct and another to Tell el-ʿAqabeh (Cypros) with bridges and tunnels; three aqueducts led Qelt water to Jericho at the end of the Second Temple period.
period: Hasmonaean (John Hyrcanus I) to end of Second Temple period
quote: The earliest aqueduct that was built in the Judaean Desert was built north of Wadi el-Qelt.

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in G.J. Brooke and P.R. Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies (2002/2004)
feature: Koziba is probably the name of the eastern Wadi el-Qelt; if the entry describes an aqueduct, it is the start of one of the Qelt aqueducts.
quote: Koziba is probably the name of the eastern part of Wadi el-Qelt

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: Five aqueducts in Wady Kelt from ʿAin Kelt and ʿAin Farah; the Jisr ed-Deir bridge where the ʿAin Kelt channels divide; near Deir el-Kelt a masonry wall built against the cliff carries two channels.
period: SWP: probably Roman or Byzantine; the bridge possibly Roman, repaired later
quote: They are probably to be ascribed to Roman times, or perhaps the Byzantine period

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Milik, J.T., DJD III (1962), section D 'Sites et monuments'
feature: Choziba was the name of the Qelt gorge from ʿAin el-Qelt to Roman Jericho; the aqueduct system, a single channel dividing into three with retaining walls, preserves the plan of the Herodian installations despite Byzantine and medieval repairs. The monastery of Choziba dates from the early 5th century.
period: Herodian plan; Byzantine and medieval repairs; monastery 5th c.
quote: a dû conserver en gros le plan des installations hérodiennes

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Puech, É., The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: Koziba is the toponym of Wadi el-Qelt 'where the water flows to this day'.

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
source: Wexler, L., 'Preface', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Most surviving systems that brought spring water to settlements and fields in the northern Judaean desert date from the Roman period onward (citing Porat; Netzer 1989 on Hasmonean aqueducts and the royal estate in the western Jericho plain).
quote: most of the systems that conveyed them to settlements and farmland survive from the Roman period onward (transl.)

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: MOUND, POOL, CHANNELS: Tell es-Sultan is an artificial double mound; Elisha's spring rises beneath it into a shallow reservoir of dressed stone, from which channels irrigate the land towards Eriha.
quote: The stream is conducted from thence by various channels, and irrigates the land between the Tell and Eriha.

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: PERIODS: ruins beside the tell (Khurbet Ras el-ʿAin, with a marble column shaft and a Byzantine-style capital) and more ruins towards Eriha; SWP places the earliest city on the tell, a Byzantine town on the lower ground, and Roman Jericho at Tulul Abu el-ʿAleik.
period: early city on the tell; Byzantine and Crusader remains around it
quote: The general impression obtained was that the earliest city must have stood on the Tell

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III: Judaea (1883)
feature: CONDUITS: aqueducts leaving ʿAin es-Sultan (one to Kh. el-Mefjir, one to Kusr el-Yehud); SWP dates the latter with Justinian's cistern and the Mefjir system to Crusader times.
quote: The grand aqueduct from the 'Ain es Sultan to it is no doubt of the same date.

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Puech, É., The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: Puech's hypothesis: Koḥlit = Tell es-Sultan, 'to the north of Hasmonaean and Herodian Jericho', with its irrigation works and spring; he lists the needed features (tell, pool to the east, large cistern and underground chamber to the north, tombs) and cites Kenyon (Excavations at Jericho III, 1981, pp.173–174, not seen here) for Qumran-type graves.
period: graves compared in type with the Qumran cemetery
quote: sepulchres of the type of those of the great cemetery of Khirbet Qumran are known from the northern side

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Sala, M., 'Tell es-Sultan (Jericho): The Archaeological Expeditions to Tell es-Sultan (1868–2012)', chapter 6 in Archaeology in the Land of 'Tells and Ruins' (Oxbow, 2014), DOI 10.2307/j.ctvh1djs1.24 (author's upload)
feature: TOMBS: Kenyon's expedition excavated over 600 tombs in the large cemetery north and west of the tell, from Early Bronze I to the Roman period (p.117); a Byzantine church stood by Elisha's spring (p.121).
quote: ranging in date from the Early Bronze Age I to the Roman Period

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Wexler, L., 'Preface', ʿAtiqot 41 (2002, Hebrew)
feature: Lists research on Jericho, including its Second Temple cemetery (Hachlili; Kenyon 1953, 1971; Hachlili and Killebrew 1999), without a location relative to the tell.

source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in G.J. Brooke and P.R. Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies (2002/2004)
feature: Hasmonaean and Herodian aqueducts fed the palace and Royal Estate south of Jericho. On I 9–12 Eshel says he cannot identify Koḥlit's aqueduct.
quote: Since little is known about Kohlit other than it was located in the desert, I cannot identify this aqueduct.

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
source: Aharonovich, Y., Hizmi, H., Orenshtein, T. and Shkolnik, H., 'Revisiting the ʿAujah Aqueducts: New Insights and Discoveries', ʿAtiqot 119 (2025) — abstract page only
feature: A Hasmonean conveyance from ʿEin el-ʿAujah, developed under Herod, supplied the winter palaces in the southern Jericho oasis; the abstract does not say whether it passed the tell.

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: C. Warren, letters of 1869 on the Golden Gate, in C. Wilson and C. Warren, The Recovery of Jerusalem (London 1871)
feature: A shaft and galleries were dug towards the Golden Gate from the east. In the debris in front of the east wall they met rock cuttings and scarps, rough masonry walls, a re-used column shaft and a massive wall of large drafted blocks.
period: No dates given for any of these remains

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: C. Warren, 'The tanks and souterrains of the Sanctuary' (building on C. Wilson's 1865 Ordnance Survey notes), in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Many rock-cut cisterns ('tanks') and underground chambers under the Haram platform, some fed by rock-cut channels. Warren tentatively links a few to Temple features named in the Mishnah.

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 51
feature: Identifies 'the East Gate' as the only eastern exit of the peribolos, the Golden Gate, rather than the Corinthian Gate or the city's east gate. Textual argument; he cites no excavation report.
quote: désigne la seule sortie orientale du péribole, la Porte Dorée

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: J. K. Lefkovits, The Copper Scroll 3Q15 (2000)
feature: The city's East Gate (Neh 3:29) and the Temple's Eastern Gate (Mishnah Middot 1:3, printed '1:13'). The unnamed city of items 9-10 is 'reasonably' Jerusalem or the Temple.

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: É. Puech, Le rouleau de cuivre (2006)
feature: The East Gate can only be that of the Jerusalem Temple, since the next entry concerns the rampart (Mishnah Middot).

place: Jerusalem, East Gate of the Temple enclosure (Golden Gate position)
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020)
feature: All the points of reference in II 3-12 (washer's house, wood-store court, eastern gate, eastern wall) point to the Temple area. Jerusalem is never named.

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: C. Warren, 'Eastern side of the Sanctuary. South-east angle' (letters of 1867-1870), in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Galleries on the western face of the Kidron below the enclosure met deep, loose shingle and debris. He describes the masonry of the east wall and its angle, and the rock it rests on.
period: No absolute dates; Warren discusses the age of the masonry only by style

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: C. Warren, letters of 1869 on the Golden Gate, in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: East of the wall near the Golden Gate the rock rises in cut scarps. Rough walls and a massive wall of drafted blocks stand in the debris.

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: C. Warren (after C. Wilson 1865), 'The tanks and souterrains of the Sanctuary', in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Rock-cut cisterns and underground chambers inside the enclosure, some with feed channels.

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 52
feature: A rocky projection under the city's east rampart, near the cache of entry 9 and north of it (Milik's own inference; he cites no report).
quote: une saillie rocheuse sous le rempart est de la ville

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: J. K. Lefkovits, The Copper Scroll 3Q15 (2000)
feature: The city wall of an unnamed city that may be Jerusalem. Cites Mishnah Kelim 1:8 for Jerusalem's wall and its inner rampart (ḥel).

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
source: É. Puech, Le rouleau de cuivre (2006)
feature: The entrance (or the cache) lies under the great threshold. The entry follows the East Gate entry.

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem (Kidron–Hinnom area or el-Baqʿa; which valley is unresolved)
source: É. Puech, Le rouleau de cuivre (2006), citing Y. Yadin, The Temple Scroll I (1983) pp. 302-303
feature: The Valley of Shaveh (Gen 14:17; 1QapGen XXII 14) is the King's Valley (2 Sam 18:18) towards Beth ha-Kerem, distinct from Josephus' Bethso south-west of the city. No archaeology is cited.
period: texts of the 2nd-1st c. BCE (1QapGen) and biblical

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem (Kidron–Hinnom area or el-Baqʿa; which valley is unresolved)
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D nos. 65-66, citing H. Vincent, Jérusalem de l'Ancien Testament I pp. 51 ff., and Josephus, BJ V §145
feature: Ha-Šoʾ = Josephus' Bethso, a necropolis south-west of Jerusalem (modern Baqʿah). Entry 36 is a north-facing hypogeum on the uncultivated west slope of a ravine. He cites no excavated tombs.
quote: Dans cette nécropole sud-ouest de Jérusalem, la moderne Baqâ'ah

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem (Kidron–Hinnom area or el-Baqʿa; which valley is unresolved)
source: C. Clermont-Ganneau, PEF Quarterly Statement 1869 p. 252, quoted in C. R. Conder and H. H. Kitchener, Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III (1883)
feature: The people of Silwan divide the Kidron into three named sections. The middle one, from the south-east angle of the Haram down to Bir Eyub, is 'Wady Fer'aun', which he glosses as the valley of the king, where the biblical King's Gardens lay.
period: 19th-century name; the link to the King's Gardens is his inference
quote: Wady Fer'aun signifies, then, the valley of the king

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem (Kidron–Hinnom area or el-Baqʿa; which valley is unresolved)
source: G. Avni and Z. Greenhut, The Akeldama Tombs: Three Burial Caves in the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem (IAA Reports 1, 1996)
page: abstract (online landing page; volume not read)
feature: The Kidron valley was one of the main burial grounds of First Temple-period Jerusalem, and many tombs were hewn there in the Second Temple period. Three large, elaborate Second Temple-period tombs, exposed during road works, held ossuaries and a sarcophagus and were reused in the Roman and Byzantine periods.
period: First and Second Temple periods; reuse in the Roman and Byzantine periods
quote: numerous tombs were also hewn here during the Second Temple period

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)
source: C. Wilson, 'The Ordnance Survey of Jerusalem, 1864-5', in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: The two pools of Siloam, at the foot of the Tyropoeon, were fed partly by surface drainage and partly from the Virgin's Fountain through an underground channel. They were probably made to irrigate the gardens below. Birket es-Sultan in the Hinnom could only have irrigated gardens lower down that valley.
quote: were probably made for the irrigation of the gardens below

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)

period: 19th-century name; the link to the King's Gardens is his inference
quote: Wady Fer'aun signifies, then, the valley of the king

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 67
feature: The irrigated part of ha-Šoʾ (C 43), placed in his south-west (Baqʿah) necropolis. The landmark is a cippus.

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)
source: É. Puech, Le rouleau de cuivre (2006); The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: 'The low irrigated part' of the (valley of) Shaveh, the counterpart of the fallow land of entry 36. No water source is named.

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020)
feature: The upper fallow terrain and the lower irrigated part of the Shaveh: 'the most meaningful interpretation'.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: O. Lipschits, M. Oeming, Y. Gadot, B. Arubas and G. Cinamon, 'Ramat Raḥel – 2005', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 118 (2006)
feature: A water system of four plastered pools, two covered plastered drains and a covered plastered rock-cut channel, in at least two phases. A large miqveh (ritual bath) was exposed nearby by Ben Dov (1963) and Barkay (1984).
period: The pool system was undated in 2005. Elsewhere the season's remains are Late Roman and Byzantine (Aharoni's Strata III-II).
quote: The system can not be dated as yet

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: O. Lipschits, M. Oeming, Y. Gadot and B. Arubas, 'The 2006 and 2007 seasons at Ramat Rahel' (preliminary report; also IEJ 59, 2009, pp. 1-20)
feature: A garden with plastered pools, decorated drains and rock-cut tunnels, which the excavators date with the palace. Later a pool was reused for slaking lime from a Hellenistic kiln. Then an intentional earth fill buried the whole garden and pool area. Later features in this part of the site are agricultural installations, tombs and a columbarium cave.
period: Garden and pools probably late Iron Age; lime kiln Hellenistic; burying fill with latest pottery of the 2nd c. BCE; later features Second Temple, Roman and Byzantine (BK: later publications by the same team put the garden in the Persian period; either way it is earlier than the 2nd-c. BCE fill)
quote: the latest of them dating to the second century BCE

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: Y. Farhi, U. Davidovich, Y. Gadot and O. Lipschits, 'The Ramat Raḥel Hoard of Tyrian Shekels', Israel Numismatic Journal 17 (2009-10)
feature: Under the Hasmoneans the site became a small Jewish settlement. Reich identified seven ritual baths among Aharoni's remains and the renewed dig found at least two more. Two columbarium caves belong to the Late Second Temple period.
period: Hasmonean–Herodian; the settlement perhaps ended after the Jewish War (Aharoni 1964 p. 121)
quote: It lost its central political and economic status and instead became a small settlement inhabited by Jews.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: I. Novoselsky, 'Ramat Raḥel', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 137 (2025)
feature: A 2015 development survey on the hill's southern slope recorded caves, hewn agricultural installations, hewn cisterns and a quarry. Two segments of Jerusalem's lower aqueduct were found next to the site in 2013 (Billig 2014).
period: Cisterns undated (only a few Iron Age and Byzantine sherds); aqueduct 'probably built by the Hasmonean kings'
quote: hewn agricultural installations, hewn cisterns and a quarry

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: J. K. Lefkovits, The Copper Scroll 3Q15 (2000), citing Y. Aharoni, 'Excavations at Ramat Rahel', BA 24 (1961) 114-117; Excavations at Ramat Rahel, Seasons 1959 and 1960 (1962) pp. 49-51, 60; Seasons 1961 and 1962 (1964) pp. 122-124
feature: Aharoni's identification argument, not a feature report. He uses the scroll's order (the great wadi, Beth-cherem, Absalom, Siloam) to place Beth-cherem near Jerusalem, and equates it with Ramat Raḥel. Lefkovits notes that Aharoni relied on Milik's preliminary version.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 29, citing Y. Aharoni, IEJ 6 (1956) 137 ff., 152-156, and BIES 24 (1960) 73-119
feature: Beth ha-Kerem 'plausibly' identified with Ramat Raḥel. Christian memory of the Virgin's Rest there from the 2nd century. The reservoir is only restated from the scroll.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: S. Pfann, in Copper Scroll Studies (2002), citing M. Stekelis, 'Une grotte funéraire juive à Ramath Rachel', Qovetz JPES (1934-35) p. 28
feature: Jar lids of the type associated with Qumran-type jars, from a Jewish burial cave at Ramat Raḥel.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
source: C. R. Conder and H. H. Kitchener, Survey of Western Palestine, Memoirs III (1883)
feature: Conder takes ʿAin Karim to be 'the true site of Beth-haccerem', and notes that Jerome put it near Tekoa. This is an alternative identification, not a feature report.

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: J. Zias, 'The "Tomb of Absalom": The Earliest Judeo-Christian Place of Pilgrimage in Jerusalem', The Ancient Near East Today (ASOR) 11.3, March 2023
feature: The standing Kidron monument called Absalom's Tomb is a square rock-cut structure with Ionic columns in relief and a conical roof, later modified and vandalized. A Greek inscription of about the 4th century CE calls it the tomb of Zacharias. Zias thinks the Copper Scroll and Josephus probably shaped the later link with Absalom.
period: Original construction 1st century CE (dated by style); inscriptions c. 4th century CE
quote: Its original construction has been dated to the 1st century CE on the basis of style

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020), citing Josephus, AJ 7.243
feature: Josephus: Absalom's monument was a marble stele or column, two stades from Jerusalem, which Absalom called his 'hand'. This is a literary description, not a site report.

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 68, citing RB 66 (1959) 550-553
feature: In the Roman period the Hand of Absalom stood in the south-west necropolis (Baqʿah), not east of the city. The argument is textual; no report is cited.

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: J. K. Lefkovits, The Copper Scroll 3Q15 (2000)
feature: The monument called Absalom's today is not the one mentioned in the Bible ('as the scholars point out').
quote: what is called today “Monument of Absalom” is not identical with the one mentioned in the Bible

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: É. Puech, The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: Places the 'valley of Job' between Beth ha-Kerem and Absalom's monument, south-east of Jerusalem (2 Sam 18:18; Josephus AJ 7.243).

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
source: G. Avni and Z. Greenhut, The Akeldama Tombs: Three Burial Caves in the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem (IAA Reports 1, 1996)
page: abstract (online landing page; volume not read)
feature: The Kidron valley was one of the main burial grounds of First Temple-period Jerusalem, and many tombs were hewn there in the Second Temple period. Three large, elaborate Second Temple-period tombs, exposed during road works, held ossuaries and a sarcophagus and were reused in the Roman and Byzantine periods.
period: First and Second Temple periods; reuse in the Roman and Byzantine periods
quote: numerous tombs were also hewn here during the Second Temple period

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: N. Szanton, 'Ritual Purification and Bathing: The Location and Function of Siloam Pool and Solomon's Pool in Second Temple Period Jerusalem', ʿAtiqot 113 (2023), doi:10.70967/2948-040X.1031
feature: Four Early Roman pools at the southern tip of the city. The Silwan Pool is identified with the Siloam Pool and Birkat el-Ḥamra with Solomon's Pool.
period: Early Roman; late Second Temple period
quote: used for ceremonies and ritual immersion of pilgrims arriving at the city in the late Second Temple period

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: M. Hagbi, N. Szanton, J. Uziel and A. Levy, 'Jerusalem, City of David, the Stepped Street', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 134 (2022)
feature: An Early Roman stepped street rises from the Siloam Pool to the Temple Mount, with a plaza and staircases leading down to the pool. It cites Reich and Shukron 2006 and 2007 for the pool-side plaza and street. [Note: this "Siloam Pool" is Reich and Shukron's pool at Birkat el-Ḥamra, which Szanton 2023 identifies as Solomon's Pool.]
period: Early Roman (strata from the 2nd c. BCE onward)
quote: the Stepped Street that ascends from the Siloam Pool to the Temple Mount

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: A. Levy and Y. Baruch, 'Jerusalem, City of David, the Stepped Street', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 135 (2023)
feature: The street and a Second Temple-period stone plaza by the Siloam Pool (citing Reich and Shukron 2005, Qadmoniot 130: 91-96). A 1st-century drainage channel; a destruction layer of 70 CE. [Note: this "Siloam Pool" is Reich and Shukron's pool at Birkat el-Ḥamra, which Szanton 2023 identifies as Solomon's Pool.]
quote: laid in the first century CE and led from the Siloam Pool

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: S. Mizrahi, 'Jerusalem, Silwan Grove', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 132 (2020)
feature: In the Second Temple period the city wall ran here, with water-supply systems and pools around it. A Second Temple-period pool was found nearby (Adan-Bayewitz 1979; Weksler-Bdolah 2013).
period: Second Temple period; a post-70 CE foundation above
quote: water-supply systems and pools constructed around it, the main and most important of these being the Pool of Siloam

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: S. Weksler-Bdolah and M. Hagbi, 'Jerusalem, Silwan', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 134 (2022)
feature: Near the Siloam Pool: a plastered wall of another stepped pool of the late Second Temple period, a Hasmonean-style wall, and part of the municipal drainage channel that ran between Robinson's Arch and the Siloam Pool.

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: C. Wilson, 'The Ordnance Survey of Jerusalem, 1864-5', in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: The two pools of Siloam were fed partly from the Virgin's Fountain through an underground channel and partly by surface drainage.

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 38, citing H. Vincent and F.-M. Abel, Jérusalem Nouvelle I pp. 6 ff., 34; IV pp. 880 ff.
feature: The baths of Siloam, famed for their medical and ritual use (John 9; yTaʿanit 2).

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
source: É. Puech, The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: 'Outlet' as used of the Gihon source in 2 Chr 32:30 and in the Siloam inscription ('from the source to the pool'). The trough reading is confirmed on the pre-cutting photograph DJD III pl. XLIII 3.
period: Hezekian water works (late 8th c. BCE), cited as background

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
source: C. Warren, 'Eastern side of the Sanctuary. South-east angle' (letters of 1867-1870), in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Shafts and galleries at the south-east angle of the enclosure and on the Kidron's western face below it met deep, loose shingle and debris. He describes the masonry of the angle and the rock beneath it. The chapter describes no tombs at the angle.

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
source: O. Chalaf and J. Uziel, 'Jerusalem, City of David', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 136 (2024), citing Y. Gadot 2016 on 1st-c. CE garbage disposal in the Kidron
feature: On the eastern slope of the City of David (the Kidron's western slope, south of the enclosure), Iron Age buildings lie under thick Early Roman refuse layers. These are found across that slope.
period: Refuse of the late Second Temple period (1st c. CE)
quote: urban refuse of Jerusalem, which was dumped here in the late Second Temple period

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
source: G. Avni and Z. Greenhut, The Akeldama Tombs: Three Burial Caves in the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem (IAA Reports 1, 1996)
page: abstract (online landing page; volume not read)
feature: The Kidron valley was one of the main burial grounds of First Temple-period Jerusalem, and many tombs were hewn there in the Second Temple period. Three large, elaborate Second Temple-period tombs, exposed during road works, held ossuaries and a sarcophagus and were reused in the Roman and Byzantine periods.
period: First and Second Temple periods; reuse in the Roman and Byzantine periods
quote: numerous tombs were also hewn here during the Second Temple period

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D nos. 40-41 and 54, citing J. Jeremias, Heiligengräber in Jesu Umwelt (1958) pp. 62-64; Hegesippus in Eusebius, HE 2.23.18; Josephus AJ 20.221
feature: Places the tomb of Zadok on the west bank of the Kidron below the south-east corner of the enclosure, opposite the three monuments still standing on the east bank. He rejects Jeremias's view that it is one of them. The argument is from texts and traditions; no excavated tomb is cited.
period: 1st c. CE (Solomon's Portico: John, Acts, Josephus)
quote: en face des trois monuments conservés jusqu'à nos jours

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020)
feature: The tomb of Zadok is described as a monumental structure with a vestibule and courtyard in the Kidron, not far from Siloam. The portico may be Solomon's Portico, which crowned the eastern wall of the enclosure.

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D (Jerusalem introduction) and no. 41
feature: The cache lies across the torrent from the tomb of Zadok, beside the standing east-bank monuments. This is Milik's placement from the text, not a site report.
quote: là où l'on admire encore aujourd'hui l'hypogée des Bene Hezir et les monuments voisins

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
source: J. Zias, 'The "Tomb of Absalom": The Earliest Judeo-Christian Place of Pilgrimage in Jerusalem', The Ancient Near East Today (ASOR) 11.3, March 2023
feature: One of the standing monuments on the Kidron's east side, 'Absalom's Tomb', is a rock-cut funerary structure with Ionic columns in relief. Its 4th-century inscriptions name Zacharias.

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
source: G. Avni and Z. Greenhut, The Akeldama Tombs: Three Burial Caves in the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem (IAA Reports 1, 1996)
page: abstract (online landing page; volume not read)
feature: The Kidron valley was one of the main burial grounds of First Temple-period Jerusalem, and many tombs were hewn there in the Second Temple period. Three large, elaborate Second Temple-period tombs, exposed during road works, held ossuaries and a sarcophagus and were reused in the Roman and Byzantine periods.
period: First and Second Temple periods; reuse in the Roman and Byzantine periods
quote: numerous tombs were also hewn here during the Second Temple period

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
source: É. Puech, The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: Mentions the tomb of the Benê Ḥezîr, a priestly family, in the Joshaphat-Kidron valley, in the discussion of entry 54.

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020)
feature: The third hoard lies outside the tomb, at the top of a rock opposite the monument. The tomb serves as the point of orientation.

place: Pools of Bethesda (St Anne's), north of the Temple enclosure
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D no. 44, citing H. Vincent and F.-M. Abel, Jérusalem Nouvelle IV (1926) pp. 669 ff., and J. Jeremias, Die Wiederentdeckung von Bethesda (1949)
feature: Essentially a large, double rectangular reservoir. The larger basin is the southern one and the smaller the northern one. Eusebius knows twin pools and the Bordeaux Pilgrim piscinae gemellares.
period: 1st c. CE (John 5:2); 4th c. CE (Eusebius, Bordeaux Pilgrim)
quote: un grand réservoir rectangulaire ... et évidemment double

place: Pools of Bethesda (St Anne's), north of the Temple enclosure
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020), citing J. Jeremias, The Rediscovery of Bethesda (1966)
feature: Two pools with five porticos at the site of the later St Anne's church, confirmed by excavations.
period: 1st c. CE (John 5:2); excavated in the late 19th and early 20th centuries
quote: excavations in the late 19th and early 20th century have confirmed the existence of two pools

place: Pools of Bethesda (St Anne's), north of the Temple enclosure
source: É. Puech, The Copper Scroll Revisited (2015)
feature: At Bethesda the smaller of the two reservoirs is the northern one, and there are other small basins that are easier to 'enter'. The location is 'not completely certain'.

place: Pools of Bethesda (St Anne's), north of the Temple enclosure
source: C. Wilson and C. Warren, The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Before the St Anne's pools were excavated, Wilson knew only a tradition of a pool near St Anne's (p. 21). Warren took the twin pools of Eusebius and the Bordeaux Pilgrim to be the rock-cut double pool, later vaulted, at the Sisters of Sion convent north-west of the Haram (pp. 196-197).
quote: pools cut in the rock, side by side, with a pier of masonry

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: E. Shukron and R. Reich, 'Jerusalem, Robinson's Arch', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 123 (2011)
feature: At the south-west corner of the enclosure, the Herodian expansion is traced in phases: dwellings dismantled (one with a miqveh), the corners marked and the first courses laid, a drainage channel cut around the corner, and a network of massive walls with soil fill packed between them.
period: Herodian expansion of the Temple Mount, before 70 CE
quote: A network of massive walls was built and soil fill was deposited between them.

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: C. Warren, chapters on the eastern side, south-east and north-east angles of the Sanctuary, in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: The enclosure's east wall and its south-east and north-east angles, with the rock they stand on and deep debris outside them.

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: C. Warren (after C. Wilson 1865), 'The tanks and souterrains of the Sanctuary', in The Recovery of Jerusalem (1871)
feature: Many rock-cut cisterns and underground chambers under the Haram platform, some with feed channels. Warren tentatively links some to Temple features named in the Mishnah (e.g. the House of Baptism, the gate Tadi).

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: Z. Dvira and G. Barkay, 'Jerusalem, The Temple Mount Sifting Project', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 133 (2021)
feature: Sifting of soil removed from the Temple Mount in 1996-2001. The finds include many stone vessels of the late Second Temple period and opus sectile floor-tile fragments of the Early Roman and later periods (finds out of context).
period: First Temple period to modern, including late Second Temple and Early Roman
quote: many attributed to the late Second Temple period stoneware industry

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: J. T. Milik, DJD III (1962), section D nos. 50, 53-59, 64, citing H. Vincent, Jérusalem de l'Ancien Testament II pp. 440, 441-446, 500 f.; Mishnah Middot 2:5-6, 5:4; Josephus BJ V §304
feature: Wood stores at the corners of the Women's Court and the inner court (Middot). The Esplanade as the great retaining walls and inner fills of the Herodian terrace (Vincent p. 440). Four corners of the peribolos. Alexander Jannaeus's tomb outside the north-east corner (Josephus). 'Little peristyle' as the popular name of the inner court's wall. These are textual and architectural reconstructions, not excavation reports.

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: É. Puech, Le rouleau de cuivre (2006), citing A. Kloner, 'Central Pillar Spiral Staircases in the Hellenistic Period', Eretz-Israel 25 (1996) 484-489
feature: Spiral stairs either in a tower or cut down in a pit. His parallels are Gibeon, 'baths for the priests at the Temple', and Hellenistic Marisa (Kloner). None is a report from the Temple enclosure itself.

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
source: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll (2020)
feature: The mesibbah (spiral staircase) is attested in 11QTemple XXX 4-XXXI 8 and Mishnah Middot 4:5. The Temple's wood-storage buildings appear in Middot 2:6. Both are textual.

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: Wady en-Nar (the Kidron) is an open, passable valley below Jerusalem until it bends east towards Mar Saba
quote: This valley (the ancient brook Kedron) is flanked by rounded hills, and is open and easily passable.

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: the Mar Saba monastery stands on the side of 'the gorge'; numerous rock-cut caves in the cliff face, apparently once lived in by hermits
period: monastic settlement from c. 480 CE; present buildings modern
quote: The settlement of monks dates from St. Euthymius and St. Sabas in the fifth century (circa 480).

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: the road from Jerusalem to Mar Saba runs down Wady en-Nar, with ancient wells along its course
quote: numerous ancient wells occur along the course, and this road seems to be that which led to Zuk.

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Milik, J.T., 'Le rouleau de cuivre provenant de la grotte 3Q (3Q15)', DJD III, 1962
feature: יגר is a heap of stones that can hide a burial; the scroll's three יגר stand in a valley, at a ford and at the entrance of a defile, so all beside a road or path; the gorge of the Kidron is reached shortly before Mar Saba
quote: donc tous à côté d'une route ou d'un sentier

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Puech, É., The Copper Scroll Revisited, 2015
feature: places the Kidron gorge a short distance before Mar Saba (after Milik); rejects the 'dam' sense of יגר
quote: The Kidron gorge is located a short distance before it reaches Mar Saba on the way from Jerusalem

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Eshel, H., 'Aqueducts in the Copper Scroll', in Brooke and Davies (eds), Copper Scroll Studies, 2002 (summarising Patrich, 'The Aqueducts of Hyrcania', 1989)
feature: Hyrcania's southern aqueduct began in Wadi Qidron (Wadi en-Nar) and ran through the stretch where the St Saba monastery was later built (p.95); Eshel reads the יגר of VIII 8 as the dam where this aqueduct began (p.102), although his description of the system (p.95) mentions a dam only for the northern aqueduct
period: southern aqueduct built in the Herodian period (p.97)
quote: the southern aqueduct, which was built during the Herodian period

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Dahari, U., 'Region XIV: Survey and Excavations of Caves along the Fault Escarpment from Naḥal Kidron to Naḥal Deragot', ʿAtiqot 41 (Hebrew), 2002
feature: a different stretch: where the Kidron leaves the fault escarpment near the Dead Sea, a cliff site ('Kidron (South)') of built niches, rooms and caves; the report calls the watercourse 'the canyon of Naḥal Kidron' (p.233); no public building and no water cistern were found (p.233); Dahari prefers a refuge for the people of Meṣad (Kh.) Mazin (p.239)
period: built in the 1st c. CE, busiest during the First Revolt (coins of years 2-3), abandoned right after; about three quarters of the pottery Early Roman (late 1st c. BCE to late 1st c. CE); Byzantine and Umayyad reuse (p.239)
quote: האתר נבנה במאה הא׳ לסה״נ, הגיע לשיאו בתקופת המרד הגדול (לפחות עד שנה ג׳), ונעזב מיד לאחריו.

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
source: Tal, N. and Oron, G., 'Region XIII: Survey and Excavations of Caves along the Fault Escarpment South of Qumran', ʿAtiqot 41 (Hebrew), 2002
feature: on the north bank of the lowest Kidron, at the escarpment: rock shelters and niches closed by built stone walls
period: sherds of the Chalcolithic, Iron II-III, Hellenistic and Byzantine periods; the built niches judged Byzantine, perhaps part of a small monastery (p.224)

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: a large natural cavern of several chambers at the site, reached along a rock ledge; SWP judges none of it cut by hand
quote: it does not appear that any of the excavation is artificial

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: the name Khureitun covers a great cave, the ruins beside it, a spring and the valley, after the ascetic Chariton, who founded the laura Suka there
period: late antique (Chariton's laura); no earlier use stated
quote: the name of Khureitun applied to the cave, to the adjacent ruins, to a spring, and to the valley below

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs III: Judaea, 1883
feature: Kh. Khureitun: tower, vaults and cisterns of a monastery on the edge of a precipice, and a well-built reservoir
period: ruins of the 12th century; the reservoir 'may be older', not dated
quote: it may be older than the ruins round the tower which belonged to the Crusading monastery of St. Chariton

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Milik, J.T., 'The Copper Document from Cave III, Qumran', ADAJ 4-5, 1960
feature: ha-Naṭoph = ʿAin en-Natuf in Wadi Khareitun; the spring issues from the hillside near the cave of St Chariton; the monks ascribed the spring to Chariton's prayers
quote: The spring comes out of the craggy hillside near the cave of St. Chariton.

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Milik, J.T., 'Le rouleau de cuivre provenant de la grotte 3Q (3Q15)', DJD III, 1962
feature: rock-cut dovecotes (rows of small niches in rocks or rock-cut chambers) are frequent in Palestine and Transjordan (after Dalman); talmudic texts say most pigeons sold at the Temple came from the 'Royal Mountain', the Herodium district; Milik still reads שובך here as a cave opening
period: Roman period (talmudic and Josephan texts); no dovecote at ʿAin en-Natuf is cited
quote: ne pouvaient servir qu'à l'élevage de pigeons

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Puech, É., The Copper Scroll Revisited, 2015
feature: Puech supposes a dovecote cut into the rock at the spring; his examples are Herodian dovecotes at Ḥorvat Abu Haf and Ḥorvat ʿAleq (Zissu 1995) and many underground columbaria at Maresha, none of them in the Naṭuf/Herodium area
period: Herodian (Zissu's examples); not stated for the spring
quote: one might easily take it that the dovecote is cut into the side of the rock

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Høgenhaven, J., The Cave 3 Copper Scroll, 2020
feature: dovecotes, built of wood or stone or cut in the rock, are well documented in ancient Palestine (after Dalman); no example at the spring is cited
quote: Dovecotes are amply documented in ancient Palestine.

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
source: Wexler, L., 'Preface' (מבואות), ʿAtiqot 41 (Hebrew), 2002
feature: lists a regional survey of the Herodium area led by Y. Hirschfeld (1985) among earlier surveys of the Judaean desert; that survey was not available for this check

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: on the summit: Samaritan holy places with a sacred rock draining into a deep cistern, rock-cut trenches, flights of steps, platforms, and about half a dozen cisterns filled with rubbish
period: not dated by SWP; the platforms 'may perhaps' belong to the temple ascribed to Sanballat
quote: may perhaps have formed part of the temple on Gerizim said to have been built by Sanballat

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: the northern knoll (Tell er-Ras) is cut off by a ditch and shows traces of steps on its sides and the foundations of a thick-walled building; the main summit has an octagonal church inside a fortress with a large reservoir
period: church ascribed to Zeno (474 CE or later) and fortress wall to Justinian (after 529 CE), both via Procopius; the reservoir compared with Byzantine monasteries; the knoll's steps not dated
quote: there are traces of steps on each of its four sides

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Lefkovits, J.K., The Copper Scroll 3Q15: A Reevaluation, 2000
feature: R.J. Bull's excavations at Tell er-Ras (1964, 1966) found a trench, discussed steps leading up the mountain and found six cisterns, which Lefkovits calls later (Bull's own feature-level link to the entry is not repeated here)
period: cisterns 'from a later period'; the rest not stated
quote: Although these were from a later period, there must have been cisterns at an earlier period too.

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Milik, J.T., 'Le rouleau de cuivre provenant de la grotte 3Q (3Q15)', DJD III, 1962
feature: with hedging, Milik thinks of an earlier phase of the stairway that climbed from a lower portico to the esplanade of Hadrian's temple of Zeus Hypsistos, built on the ruins of the Samaritan temple; in 36 CE Samaritans expected to find sacred vessels hidden on the mountain (Josephus AJ 18.85)
period: stairway Hadrianic (2nd c. CE); an earlier phase is Milik's hypothesis
quote: on songerait volontiers à une phase antérieure de l'escalier

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Lefkovits, J.K., The Copper Scroll 3Q15: A Reevaluation, 2000
feature: textual background: Megillat Taʿanit celebrates the capture of the wall of Samaria and a 'Day of Mount Gerizim'
period: Hasmonean conquest, late 2nd c. BCE (128 BCE for Samaria per Lefkovits)

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
source: Høgenhaven, J., The Cave 3 Copper Scroll, 2020
feature: Gerizim was the site of the Samaritan sanctuary, and Jewish and Samaritan traditions treat it as a hiding place of sacred vessels (Josephus AJ 18.85-89)

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882 (quoting E. Robinson)
feature: several large brooks pass by or through the site; the ancient city lay among abundant waters, with the ruins of Scythopolis (theatre, temples, colonnades)
period: natural watercourses; ruins Roman to Islamic
quote: Not less than four large brooks of water pass by or through the site of Beisan.

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: the city is exceptionally well watered; streams from ʿAin Malhah and ʿAin el-Melab run through the ruins; ʿAin el-Melab, 'Spring of the Playhouse', is named after the Roman theatre
period: springs natural; the theatre is called Roman work
quote: in a situation extraordinarily well supplied with water

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: ʿAin es-Soda near Beisan, a very large and apparently perennial spring
quote: a very large spring with a considerable stream and a gravelly bed

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Milik, J.T., 'Le rouleau de cuivre provenant de la grotte 3Q (3Q15)', DJD III, 1962
feature: the rare word מבוע and the lack of other directions suggest the main fountain of Beisan, probably the one described by Egeria (late 4th c.), Cyril of Scythopolis (St Sabas's visit of 518, 'En-Temane) and Abbot Daniel (12th c.)
quote: suggèrent qu'il s'agit de la fontaine principale de Beisan

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Har'el, Y., 'Bet She'an, Railway Station', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 128, 2016
feature: a dam on a tributary of Naḥal Ḥarod in the city's farmland, holding water for drinking and irrigation; a pool of the same periods found nearby (Har'el 2015)
period: Late Hellenistic and Early Roman (1st c. BCE-1st c. CE); abandoned after the Early Roman period
quote: Even where water resources are abundant, as they are in the Bet She’an Valley, farmers needed a dam

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Horowitz, Z. and Atrash, W., 'Bet She'an, Tel Iẓṭabba', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 128, 2016
feature: at Tel Iẓṭabba, on the edge of the town, the rock was laid down by the many springs of the area
period: geological; the site has Hellenistic and Roman pottery
quote: deposited by the numerous springs in the vicinity

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Tzin, B. and Najar, A., 'Bet She'an, Railway Station', Hadashot Arkheologiyot 134, 2022
feature: an underground mausoleum at the edge of the town, evidence of Early Roman activity
period: built in the second half of the 1st c. BCE, used until the 1st c. CE
quote: The mausoleum was built in the second half of the first century BCE

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
source: Milik, J.T., 'The Copper Document from Cave III, Qumran', ADAJ 4-5, 1960
feature: Bethsan-Scythopolis was a pagan city in the Graeco-Roman period with a Jewish minority of some importance

place: Kh. Ibziq (Bezek), north-east of Nablus
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: Khurbet Ibzik: traces of ruins, cisterns and caves, and a domed shrine of Sheikh Hazkin
quote: Evidently an ancient site, with traces of ruins, cisterns and caves

place: Kh. Ibziq (Bezek), north-east of Nablus
source: Conder, C.R. and Kitchener, H.H., The Survey of Western Palestine. Memoirs II: Samaria, 1882
feature: the two villages called Bezek in the Onomasticon, on the road from Neapolis to Scythopolis, are placed at Khurbet Ibzik on that road
quote: This site is evidently Khurbet Ibzik
